title: How would you debug sustained high CPU in a Java service (collect evidence first: CPU metrics, thread dumps, an async/sampling profiler: to find the hot code paths before changing anything), and what are the common causes (tight loops, expensive serialization, lock contention, pathological regex backtracking, and GC pressure)?
shortTitle: How would you debug sustained high CPU in a Java service, and what are the common causes
keyPoints: Always collect evidence with CPU metrics, thread dumps, and a sampling profiler before changing any code.
The first split is application CPU versus garbage-collection CPU because their fixes are opposite.
An async or sampling profiler produces a flame graph that names the hottest methods directly.
Common causes are tight loops, expensive serialization, lock contention, regex backtracking, and GC pressure.
Each cause has a distinct fingerprint in the flame graph or thread dump that guides the fix.
Never scale out a CPU-bound service before proving the root cause, because scaling a defect just burns more money.
High CPU and high latency are different problems: a slow service with idle CPU is waiting, not computing.

s1_definition.oneliner: Debug high CPU by first proving which threads and methods are burning it with CPU metrics, GC separation, and an async profiler, then fix the proven cause, usually a tight loop, expensive serialization, lock contention, regex backtracking, or GC pressure.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Evidence first** – Collect CPU metrics per instance, separate application CPU from GC CPU, and run an async or sampling profiler to produce a flame graph before touching any code.
- **GC split** – If a large fraction of CPU is in garbage collection with the heap filling repeatedly, the cause is allocation pressure, not business logic.
- **Flame graph** – The profiler samples thread stacks at high frequency and names the hottest methods as the widest bars, removing all guesswork.
- **Common causes** – Tight loops or bad algorithms, expensive JSON or object serialization, lock contention showing as spinning threads, pathological regex backtracking, and GC pressure from excessive short-lived allocation.
- **Fix the proven cause** – Each cause has a distinct fingerprint and a specific fix; scaling out without diagnosis just multiplies a defect across more machines.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine one teller at National Bank of India is sweating and working furiously non-stop, yet the queue barely moves. A reckless manager would just hire more tellers. A systematic manager watches exactly what that teller is doing over and over: is he re-counting the same stack of notes in an endless loop, is he laboriously re-writing a huge form, is he fighting with a colleague over a single shared ledger, or is he constantly cleaning his desk because he runs out of space (the garbage-collection equivalent). You observe the busy worker, find the one wasteful task, and fix that specific task.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Debugging sustained high CPU in a Java service always starts with collecting evidence before touching any code. At National Bank of India, when the fraud-detection service pinned every core and stayed pinned even after traffic dropped, the team wanted to add instances. Pankaj insisted on profiling first. The first step was confirming whether GC was the culprit using GC logs, which it was not, so the CPU was genuinely in application code. Running async-profiler for 30 seconds produced a flame graph that put 72 percent of CPU inside the regex matcher used to validate transaction narrations.

The common causes each have a distinct fingerprint. A tight loop or bad algorithm shows one business method dominating the flame graph. Expensive serialization shows Jackson or mapper frames on top. Lock contention shows many threads BLOCKED on the same monitor in a thread dump. Pathological regex backtracking shows the regex matcher pinning a core on a single request. GC pressure shows high GC CPU and allocation rate rather than business frames. In Rajesh's case, it was classic catastrophic backtracking caused by a pattern with nested quantifiers hitting a crafted long narration input.

The fix was rewriting the regex to use a possessive quantifier and bounding the input length, which dropped the validation from seconds to microseconds and CPU returned to normal. The lesson Pankaj teaches every junior engineer is: never fix before you measure, prefer a sampling profiler over manual thread dumps, correlate the onset with the deploy that introduced the new code, and capture evidence before restarting because a restart hides the cause.

Remember one sentence: Debug high CPU by proving which threads and methods burn it with an async profiler, split app CPU from GC CPU, then fix the proven cause, which is almost always a tight loop, expensive serialization, lock contention, regex backtracking, or GC pressure.
